ACCESSORY DWELLING UNIT / JUNIOR ACCESSORY DWELLING UNIT MINISTERIAL APPROVAL — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814

ACCESSORY DWELLING UNIT APPLICATION — PROJECT IDENTIFICATION
ACCESSORY DWELLING UNIT / JUNIOR ACCESSORY DWELLING UNIT — PROJECT INFORMATION
(Referencing California Government Code Chapter 13, commencing with Section 66310, governing ministerial local-agency approval of accessory dwelling units and junior accessory dwelling units)

Property Owner: Jordan Lee
Property Address: 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814
Local Agency (city, county, or city and county with permitting jurisdiction over the property): City of Sacramento

Description of Proposed Unit (attached ADU, detached ADU, ADU converted from existing space, or junior accessory dwelling unit; approximate size; and whether it will share sanitation facilities with the primary dwelling, if applicable): _______________________________________________

Date Application Submitted to Local Agency: _______________________________________________

This sheet identifies the property, the owner, and the local agency for reference in connection with an accessory dwelling unit or junior accessory dwelling unit application. It states facts for identification purposes only; it does not itself constitute or substitute for the permit application that must be submitted to, and acted on by, the local agency, and it does not determine whether the proposed unit qualifies for ministerial approval under any particular provision of Chapter 13.

MINISTERIAL APPROVAL REQUIREMENT AND THE STATUTORY TIMELINE
California law requires a local agency's permitting agency to consider and approve a qualifying accessory dwelling unit (ADU) application ministerially -- without discretionary review or a public hearing -- notwithstanding certain other statutes governing variances or special use permits and notwithstanding any local ordinance regulating the issuance of variances or special use permits. The permitting agency must determine whether an application is complete, and give the applicant written notice of that determination, within 15 business days of receiving the application; if it is incomplete, the agency must identify what is missing so the applicant can cure it, and a resubmission is subject to the same 15-business-day completeness-determination timeline. Once an application is complete, the permitting agency must approve or deny it within 60 days if the lot already has an existing single-family or multifamily dwelling; if the ADU application is submitted together with an application to build a new primary dwelling on the same lot, the agency may delay acting on the ADU application until it acts on the new-dwelling application (or, if the applicant requests a delay, the 60-day period is tolled), but the ADU application must still be considered without discretionary review or a hearing. If the local agency does not approve or deny a completed application within the applicable 60-day period, the application is deemed approved by operation of law. If the agency denies an application, it must return a full set of written comments, within the same time period, listing the application's specific defects or deficiencies and how they can be remedied. No local ordinance, policy, or regulation other than an ADU ordinance consistent with this article of the statute may serve as the basis for delaying or denying an ADU building or use permit under this ministerial process. A denied or incomplete-determination decision may be appealed in writing to the agency's governing body (or, for a city or county, at the applicant's option, to the planning commission as well), and the agency must issue a final written determination on that appeal within 60 business days of receiving it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A permit application for an accessory dwelling unit shall be considered and approved ministerially without discretionary review or a hearing, notwithstanding Section 65901 or 65906 or any local ordinance regulating the issuance of variances or special use permits."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66317(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66317.)
  "The permitting agency shall either approve or deny the application to create or serve an accessory dwelling unit within 60 days from the date the permitting agency receives a completed application if there is an existing single-family or multifamily dwelling on the lot."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66317(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66317.)
  "If the local agency has not approved or denied the completed application within 60 days, the application shall be deemed approved."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66317(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66317.)
  "A permitting agency shall determine whether an application to create or serve an accessory dwelling unit is complete and provide written notice of this determination to the applicant not later than 15 business days after the permitting agency received the application."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66317(a)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66317.)
  "No local ordinance, policy, or regulation, other than an accessory dwelling unit ordinance consistent with this article shall be the basis for the delay or denial of a building permit or a use permit under this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(c) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66317(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66317.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66317 as currently in effect. This statute was substantially recodified, effective March 25, 2024 (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)), out of former Government Code section 65852.2 -- a former section number that a reader may encounter in older summaries, articles, or even older versions of this project's own content, and that no longer contains this law. Section 66317 was itself amended again in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 520 (SB 543)), effective January 1, 2026. Because this area of law changes frequently, a reader should confirm, at the time of use, that no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the core ministerial-review mandate and the completeness/approval/appeal timelines in section 66317; it does not cover every procedural detail in that section (for example, the local agency's authority to charge an implementation-cost fee), and it does not address the separate, distinct approval pathways and conditions found elsewhere in this chapter (including the specific unit types described in Government Code section 66323, addressed only in a separate clause of this document). It does not determine whether a particular application is in fact complete, whether a particular local agency's actions complied with these timelines, or whether a particular denial was lawful.

STATUTORY LIMITS ON A LOCAL ADU ORDINANCE'S LOT-SIZE, UNIT-SIZE, AND HEIGHT STANDARDS
A local agency's own ADU ordinance may impose objective standards -- including parking, height, setback, landscaping, architectural review, and maximum unit size -- but the statute expressly forbids one of those categories outright: an ordinance may not include any minimum-lot-size requirement for an ADU. On unit size, a local agency may set both minimum and maximum size limits, but a maximum may not be set below 850 square feet of interior livable space (or below 1,000 square feet of interior livable space for a unit with more than one bedroom), and a minimum size requirement may not be set so as to prohibit an efficiency unit. Separately, the statute caps the size of a detached ADU created under a local ordinance at 1,200 square feet of total floor area, and caps an attached ADU at 50% of the existing primary dwelling's total floor area. On height, a local ordinance's height limitation may not be set below specific statutory floors that vary by circumstance: at least 16 feet for a detached ADU on a lot with an existing or proposed single-family or multifamily dwelling; at least 18 feet (plus an additional two feet to accommodate a roof pitch aligned with the primary dwelling's) for a detached ADU within one-half mile walking distance of a major transit stop or high-quality transit corridor, or for a detached ADU on a lot with an existing or proposed multifamily, multistory dwelling; and, for an ADU attached to a primary dwelling, at least 25 feet or the height limit that otherwise applies to the primary dwelling under the local zoning ordinance, whichever is lower (without a local agency being required to allow more than two stories).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Impose objective standards on accessory dwelling units that include, but are not limited to, parking, height, setback, landscape, architectural review, maximum size of a unit, and standards that prevent adverse impacts on any real property that is listed in the California Register of Historical Resources. These standards shall not include requirements on minimum lot size."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66314(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66314(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66314.)
  "A maximum square footage requirement for either an attached or detached accessory dwelling unit that is less than either of the following: (A) Eight hundred fifty square feet of interior livable space. (B) One thousand square feet of interior livable space for an accessory dwelling unit that provides more than one bedroom."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66321(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66321(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66321.)
  "If there is an existing primary dwelling, the total floor area of an attached accessory dwelling unit shall not exceed 50 percent of the existing primary dwelling. (5) The total floor area for a detached accessory dwelling unit shall not exceed 1,200 square feet."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66314(d)(4)-(d)(5) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66314(d)(4)-(d)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66314.)
  "Any height limitation that does not allow at least the following, as applicable: (A) A height of 16 feet for a detached accessory dwelling unit on a lot with an existing or proposed single family or multifamily dwelling unit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66321(b)(4)(A)-(D) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66321(b)(4)(A)-(D) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66321.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code sections 66314 and 66321 as currently in effect, both part of the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.2, and both since amended in 2025 (section 66314 by Stats. 2025, ch. 67 (AB 1170); section 66321 by Stats. 2025, ch. 520 (SB 543)), effective January 1, 2026. A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause addresses only the lot-size, unit-size, and height limits found in these two sections; it does not cover every objective standard a local ordinance may otherwise impose (for example, architectural review or landscaping standards), does not cover the separate ministerial size allowances that apply notwithstanding a local ordinance under a different statute (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and does not determine whether a specific local agency's ordinance in fact complies with these statutory floors and ceilings.

STATUTORY LIMITS ON LOCAL PARKING REQUIREMENTS FOR ADUS
California law bars a local agency, whether or not it has adopted its own ADU ordinance, from imposing any parking requirement for an ADU in a defined set of circumstances -- among them, when the ADU is within one-half mile walking distance of public transit, when it is within an architecturally and historically significant historic district, when it is part of the existing or proposed primary residence or an accessory structure, when required on-street parking permits are not offered to the ADU's occupant, or when a car-share vehicle is located within one block of the ADU. Separately, when a local agency's ordinance does impose a parking requirement outside those circumstances, the statute caps it at one parking space per ADU or per bedroom, whichever is less, and that space may be provided as tandem parking on a driveway; off-street parking must be permitted in setback areas or as tandem parking unless the agency makes specific findings that doing so is not feasible based on site-specific or regional topographical, fire, or life-safety conditions. When an existing garage, carport, covered parking structure, or uncovered parking space is demolished or converted to create an ADU, the local agency may not require those parking spaces to be replaced.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A local agency shall not impose any parking standards for an accessory dwelling unit in any of the following instances: (1) Where the accessory dwelling unit is located within one-half of one mile walking distance of public transit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66322(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66322(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66322.)
  "Parking requirements for accessory dwelling units shall not exceed one parking space per accessory dwelling unit or per bedroom, whichever is less. These spaces may be provided as tandem parking on a driveway."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66314(d)(10)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66314(d)(10)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66314.)
  "When a garage, carport, covered parking structure, or uncovered parking space is demolished in conjunction with the construction of an accessory dwelling unit or converted to an accessory dwelling unit, the local agency shall not require that those offstreet parking spaces be replaced."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66314(d)(11) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66314(d)(11) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66314.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code sections 66322 and 66314(b)(2) and (d)(10)-(11), as currently in effect, both part of the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.2; section 66314 was further amended in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 67 (AB 1170)), effective January 1, 2026. A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the parking-specific limits in these provisions; it does not catalog every listed exemption in section 66322(a) verbatim (for example, the exemption for an ADU submitted together with a new-dwelling application on the same lot is only summarized here, not quoted), and it does not determine whether a specific property in fact falls within any exemption (for instance, whether a specific location is within one-half mile of public transit as the statute defines that term).

NO OWNER-OCCUPANCY REQUIREMENT MAY BE IMPOSED ON AN ADU
For an accessory dwelling unit created under a local agency's ADU ordinance, current California law states that the size, setback, parking, height, and other standards a local agency's ordinance may impose are the maximum standards the agency may use, and that no additional standard -- expressly including an owner-occupancy requirement -- may be imposed. The one exception the statute itself carves out is that a local agency may still require that the property be used only for rentals of terms of 30 days or longer. This is a distinct rule from the one that applies to a junior accessory dwelling unit, which (as described in a separate clause of this document) does carry a conditional owner-occupancy requirement in some circumstances.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Section 66314 establishes the maximum standards that a local agency shall use to evaluate a proposed accessory dwelling unit on a lot that includes a proposed or existing single-family dwelling. No additional standards, other than those provided in Section 66314, shall be used or imposed, including an owner-occupant requirement, except that a local agency may require that the property may be used for rentals of terms 30 days or longer."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66315 (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66315 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66315.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66315, added in the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.2, and unamended since. This is a narrow, single-sentence statute, and this clause states it in full; it does not address the minimum-30-day-rental-term condition in any further depth, does not address whether a property owner's other obligations (for example, under any applicable short-term-rental ordinance) might independently affect how the unit can be used, and does not address the different, conditional owner-occupancy rule that applies to a junior accessory dwelling unit rather than an accessory dwelling unit as such.

JUNIOR ACCESSORY DWELLING UNIT: STATUTORY SIZE CAP AND SHARED SANITATION FACILITIES
California law defines a junior accessory dwelling unit (JADU) -- a category distinct from an accessory dwelling unit -- as a unit of no more than 500 square feet of interior livable space, contained entirely within a single-family residence (enclosed space such as an attached garage counts as part of the residence for this purpose). A JADU may include its own separate sanitation facilities, or it may instead share sanitation facilities with the rest of the existing structure. A local agency's JADU ordinance must also require a permitted JADU to include a separate entrance from the main entrance of the single-family residence, and to include an efficiency kitchen with a cooking facility with appliances and a food preparation counter and storage cabinets of reasonable size for the unit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Junior accessory dwelling unit” means a unit that is no more than 500 square feet of interior livable space in size and contained entirely within a single-family residence. A junior accessory dwelling unit may include separate sanitation facilities, or may share sanitation facilities with the existing structure."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66313(d) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66313(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66313.)
  "Require the permitted junior accessory dwelling unit to include an efficiency kitchen, which shall include all of the following: (1) A cooking facility with appliances. (2) A food preparation counter and storage cabinets that are of reasonable size in relation to the size of the junior accessory dwelling unit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(f) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66333(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66333.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code sections 66313(d) and 66333, both part of the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.22; section 66313 was further amended in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 520 (SB 543)) and section 66333 in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 507 (AB 1154)), both effective January 1, 2026. A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the JADU size definition and the shared-sanitation and entrance/kitchen features; the JADU's separate, conditional owner-occupancy rule is addressed in a separate clause of this document, and this clause does not address the required deed restriction, the one-JADU-per-lot limit, or every other condition a JADU ordinance must include under section 66333.

JUNIOR ACCESSORY DWELLING UNIT: OWNER-OCCUPANCY REQUIREMENT DEPENDS ON SHARED SANITATION
Unlike an accessory dwelling unit -- for which, as described in a separate clause of this document, no owner-occupancy requirement may be imposed at all -- a junior accessory dwelling unit (JADU) is subject to a conditional owner-occupancy rule under current California law. If a local agency's JADU ordinance permits a JADU to share sanitation facilities with the existing structure, that ordinance must require owner-occupancy of the single-family residence in which the JADU is located; the statute specifies that the owner may satisfy this by living in either the remaining portion of the structure or the newly created JADU itself. Owner-occupancy is not required, however, if the JADU instead has its own separate sanitation facilities, or if the owner is a governmental agency, land trust, or housing organization rather than an individual. A local agency's JADU ordinance must also require recordation of a running-with-the-land deed restriction addressing both a prohibition on selling the JADU separately from the single-family residence and a restriction on the JADU's size and attributes, and must require that any rental of a JADU be for a term longer than 30 days.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If the junior accessory dwelling unit has shared sanitation facilities with the existing structure, require owner-occupancy in the single family residence in which the junior accessory dwelling unit will be permitted. The owner may reside in either the remaining portion of the structure or the newly created junior accessory dwelling unit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(b) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66333(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66333.)
  "Owner-occupancy shall not be required if the junior accessory dwelling unit has separate sanitation facilities, or if the owner is another governmental agency, land trust, or housing organization."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(b) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66333(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66333.)
  "Require the recordation of a deed restriction, which shall run with the land, shall be filed with the permitting agency, and shall include both of the following: (1) A prohibition on the sale of the junior accessory dwelling unit separate from the sale of the single-family residence, including a statement that the deed restriction may be enforced against future purchasers."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(c) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66333(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66333.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66333, part of the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.22, and further amended in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 507 (AB 1154)), effective January 1, 2026. A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the conditional owner-occupancy rule and the deed-restriction and minimum-rental-term requirements in section 66333; it does not address the one-JADU-per-lot limit, the requirement that a JADU be built within the walls of the residence, the separate-entrance requirement, or the efficiency-kitchen requirement, all addressed only in part (or not at all) elsewhere in this document, and it does not determine whether a specific JADU's sanitation facilities in fact qualify as "shared" or "separate" under the statute, or whether a specific owner in fact qualifies for the governmental-agency, land-trust, or housing-organization exception.

expectedJSON.body: California law bars a local agency, whether or not it has adopted its own ADU ordinance, from imposing any parking requirement for an ADU in a defined set of circumstances -- among them, when the ADU is within one-half mile walking distance of public transit, when it is within an architecturally and historically significant historic district, when it is part of the existing or proposed primary residence or an accessory structure, when required on-street parking permits are not offered to the ADU's occupant, or when a car-share vehicle is located within one block of the ADU. Separately, when a local agency's ordinance does impose a parking requirement outside those circumstances, the statute caps it at one parking space per ADU or per bedroom, whichever is less, and that space may be provided as tandem parking on a driveway; off-street parking must be permitted in setback areas or as tandem parking unless the agency makes specific findings that doing so is not feasible based on site-specific or regional topographical, fire, or life-safety conditions. When an existing garage, carport, covered parking structure, or uncovered parking space is demolished or converted to create an ADU, the local agency may not require those parking spaces to be replaced.

citations.quote: A local agency shall not impose any parking standards for an accessory dwelling unit in any of the following instances: (1) Where the accessory dwelling unit is located within one-half of one mile walking distance of public transit.

citations.quote: Parking requirements for accessory dwelling units shall not exceed one parking space per accessory dwelling unit or per bedroom, whichever is less. These spaces may be provided as tandem parking on a driveway.

citations.quote: When a garage, carport, covered parking structure, or uncovered parking space is demolished in conjunction with the construction of an accessory dwelling unit or converted to an accessory dwelling unit, the local agency shall not require that those offstreet parking spaces be replaced.

expectedJSON.body: For an accessory dwelling unit created under a local agency's ADU ordinance, current California law states that the size, setback, parking, height, and other standards a local agency's ordinance may impose are the maximum standards the agency may use, and that no additional standard -- expressly including an owner-occupancy requirement -- may be imposed. The one exception the statute itself carves out is that a local agency may still require that the property be used only for rentals of terms of 30 days or longer. This is a distinct rule from the one that applies to a junior accessory dwelling unit, which (as described in a separate clause of this document) does carry a conditional owner-occupancy requirement in some circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66315 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Section 66314 establishes the maximum standards that a local agency shall use to evaluate a proposed accessory dwelling unit on a lot that includes a proposed or existing single-family dwelling. No additional standards, other than those provided in Section 66314, shall be used or imposed, including an owner-occupant requirement, except that a local agency may require that the property may be used for rentals of terms 30 days or longer.

expectedJSON.body: California law defines a junior accessory dwelling unit (JADU) -- a category distinct from an accessory dwelling unit -- as a unit of no more than 500 square feet of interior livable space, contained entirely within a single-family residence (enclosed space such as an attached garage counts as part of the residence for this purpose). A JADU may include its own separate sanitation facilities, or it may instead share sanitation facilities with the rest of the existing structure. A local agency's JADU ordinance must also require a permitted JADU to include a separate entrance from the main entrance of the single-family residence, and to include an efficiency kitchen with a cooking facility with appliances and a food preparation counter and storage cabinets of reasonable size for the unit.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66313(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Junior accessory dwelling unit” means a unit that is no more than 500 square feet of interior livable space in size and contained entirely within a single-family residence. A junior accessory dwelling unit may include separate sanitation facilities, or may share sanitation facilities with the existing structure.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Require the permitted junior accessory dwelling unit to include an efficiency kitchen, which shall include all of the following: (1) A cooking facility with appliances. (2) A food preparation counter and storage cabinets that are of reasonable size in relation to the size of the junior accessory dwelling unit.

A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the JADU size definition and the shared-sanitation and entrance/kitchen features; the JADU's separate, conditional owner-occupancy rule is addressed in a separate clause of this document, and this clause does not address the required deed restriction, the one-JADU-per-lot limit, or every other condition a JADU ordinance must include under section 66333.

expectedJSON.body: Unlike an accessory dwelling unit -- for which, as described in a separate clause of this document, no owner-occupancy requirement may be imposed at all -- a junior accessory dwelling unit (JADU) is subject to a conditional owner-occupancy rule under current California law. If a local agency's JADU ordinance permits a JADU to share sanitation facilities with the existing structure, that ordinance must require owner-occupancy of the single-family residence in which the JADU is located; the statute specifies that the owner may satisfy this by living in either the remaining portion of the structure or the newly created JADU itself. Owner-occupancy is not required, however, if the JADU instead has its own separate sanitation facilities, or if the owner is a governmental agency, land trust, or housing organization rather than an individual. A local agency's JADU ordinance must also require recordation of a running-with-the-land deed restriction addressing both a prohibition on selling the JADU separately from the single-family residence and a restriction on the JADU's size and attributes, and must require that any rental of a JADU be for a term longer than 30 days.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the junior accessory dwelling unit has shared sanitation facilities with the existing structure, require owner-occupancy in the single family residence in which the junior accessory dwelling unit will be permitted. The owner may reside in either the remaining portion of the structure or the newly created junior accessory dwelling unit.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Owner-occupancy shall not be required if the junior accessory dwelling unit has separate sanitation facilities, or if the owner is another governmental agency, land trust, or housing organization.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Require the recordation of a deed restriction, which shall run with the land, shall be filed with the permitting agency, and shall include both of the following: (1) A prohibition on the sale of the junior accessory dwelling unit separate from the sale of the single-family residence, including a statement that the deed restriction may be enforced against future purchasers.
